summary:
A trans visitor to Nariño department stands under the national framework of Colombia, which is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; the official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on self-recognition without a surgical requirement, marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025. Courts have also intervened in detention, ruling on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty and protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025, and one report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, welcoming the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that killings are rising.

Targeted killing of trans women continues in ordinary urban settings. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, in April 2025; a 28-second video of the assault went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands, flailing in a creek unable to swim before she drowned, and she died the following afternoon. No one was arrested although police interrogated local residents. President Gustavo Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities to denounce transphobia; her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was".

Where armed groups operate, the violence takes the form of announced campaigns. In Caquetá, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns publicised through street and WhatsApp flyers naming "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots", "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign by groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. Three armed men gave the trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, one week to leave town or be killed; she hid for a week and fled at night. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Trans women in Caquetá reported few options beyond sex work, with discrimination limiting trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity; the UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

National figures of this kind cover Nariño, but no department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding was located for Nariño itself, and the 2025 national reporting flags it neither for a public-order regime nor for territorial expansion of anti-LGBTIQ+ violence.

Caquetá is the clearest documented example of armed-group "social cleansing" activity, and the pattern of flyers, threats and forced displacement there resembles the Guajira kill-list flyers of March 2024; whether either pattern extends into Nariño is not sourced.

Earlier fatal attacks in Colombia include gay men lured through an app and killed, a trans rough-sleeper stabbed while sleeping, and people killed in their homes or in a hairdresser, indicating that risk is not confined to areas under armed-group control.

Economic marginality compounds physical risk: discrimination confines trans women largely to hairdressing and sex work, and in Caquetá trans women reported few options beyond sex work, exposing them to the groups issuing the threats.

Armed groups responsible for the campaigns continue to operate despite the 2016 peace agreement.

Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and courts have ruled on the treatment of trans detainees in the prison system.
